name: Psychology Foundations
description: A foundational survey of psychology as a science, the nervous system, sensation and perception, consciousness, learning, memory, thinking and language, and intelligence for beginning students.

modules.title: Introduction to Psychology
modules.objectives: Define psychology as a science, trace its historical roots, identify major theoretical perspectives, and describe career paths in the field.
modules.readingNote: Read OpenStax Psychology 2e §1.2 for Wundt (Leipzig laboratory, 1879), structuralism, functionalism, behaviorism, humanism, and the cognitive revolution. Also read §1.1 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/1-1-what-is-psychology for psychology as the scientific study of behavior and mental processes; §1.3 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/1-3-contemporary-psychology for current perspectives; and §1.4 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/1-4-careers-in-psychology for research, applied, and clinical career paths. Working distinction: biological accounts examine neural processes; psychodynamic accounts propose unconscious conflicts; behavioral accounts examine learned consequences; cognitive accounts examine attention and interpretation; humanistic accounts emphasize agency and growth. A perspective suggests a testable explanation, not a diagnosis.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Introduction to Psychology. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.video2Note: Crash Course Psychology #1 — introductory overview of psychology and its major perspectives.
modules.practiceNote: Read §2.2 and the experimental-design discussion in §2.3 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/2-3-analyzing-findings. Worked model: randomly assign music or silence (independent variable), measure words recalled (dependent variable), and hold study time constant. Random assignment helps balance prior differences; random sampling concerns population representation. A controlled experiment can support causation; an association alone cannot. For Jordan, a behavioral hypothesis is that relief reinforces checking; a cognitive hypothesis is that an error is interpreted as failure. These are competing inferences, not established causes. Practice: name a controlled observation that could distinguish them. Then complete the supplied fictional assignment; no login, paid service, or personal health disclosure is required.
modules.assignment: Use this fictional observation: During a difficult online practice set, Jordan checks a phone after every error; notifications occur unpredictably, and checking briefly reduces frustration. Submit: a 450–550-word comparison explaining the behavior from any two of these perspectives—biological, psychodynamic, behavioral, cognitive, or humanistic—and then state which explanation is better supported by the supplied facts. Include: each perspective's mechanism, at least two facts from the case for each analysis, one fact neither perspective can explain confidently, and a proposed observation that could distinguish the explanations. Do not diagnose Jordan or disclose personal mental-health information. Evaluation: The teacher checks accurate use of both perspectives, separation of observation from inference, use of the supplied evidence, and a justified conclusion.

modules.title: Brain & Nervous System
modules.objectives: Describe the structure and function of neurons, explain synaptic transmission, and identify the roles of major brain regions in behavior and mental processes.
modules.readingNote: Read §3.2 for dendrites, cell body, axon, myelin, terminals, action potentials, neurotransmitter release, and reuptake. Also read §3.3 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/3-3-parts-of-the-nervous-system for central/peripheral and autonomic divisions, §3.4 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/3-4-the-brain-and-spinal-cord for brain regions, and §8.2 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/8-2-parts-of-the-brain-involved-with-memory for hippocampus and amygdala. A typical neuron rests near -70 mV; an action potential propagates along its axon, triggering neurotransmitter release across a synapse. Reuptake returns transmitter to the releasing cell. The hippocampus supports new episodic memories; the amygdala contributes to threat learning; frontal regions support planning; brainstem circuits support arousal and vital functions.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Brain & Nervous System. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.video2Note: Crash Course Anatomy & Physiology #8 — nervous-system structures and signaling.
modules.practiceNote: Worked pathway: horn sound -> auditory receptors -> sensory pathways -> brainstem startle circuits -> somatic motor output to muscles. Parallel brain threat/arousal networks can recruit sympathetic autonomic output to raise heart rate; parasympathetic activity supports recovery. The spinal cord carries many body signals and reflex pathways, but the horn response is not simply a spinal withdrawal reflex. Practice: draw separate arrows for muscle startle and autonomic arousal, then explain why memory difficulty alone cannot locate a specific lesion. Then complete the supplied fictional assignment; no login, paid service, or personal health disclosure is required.
modules.assignment: Use this fictional case: After a bicycle fall, Sam can speak and move normally but has difficulty forming new episodic memories; hearing a sudden horn still produces a rapid startle response and increased heart rate. Submit: a labeled two-part diagram and a 350–450-word explanation. Include: a neuron labeled dendrites, cell body, axon, myelin, terminals, and synapse; a brain/body map labeling hippocampus, amygdala, frontal lobe, brainstem, spinal cord, and sympathetic nervous system; arrows showing the likely pathway for the startle response; and a cautious explanation of which structures relate to the memory difficulty. Evaluation: The teacher checks anatomical accuracy, signal direction, correct structure-function links, and whether claims stay within the evidence rather than diagnosing the fictional person.

modules.title: Sensation & Perception
modules.objectives: Distinguish sensation from perception, apply Weber's Law and signal detection theory, and explain key Gestalt principles and top-down vs. bottom-up processing.
modules.readingNote: Read §5.1 for sensation, perception, transduction, thresholds, top-down/bottom-up processing, and signal detection; add §5.3 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/5-3-vision for depth cues and §5.6 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/5-6-gestalt-principles-of-perception for Gestalt grouping. Closure completes missing contours; proximity groups nearby elements; similarity groups matching features; good continuation favors smooth paths. An absolute threshold is detection on 50% of trials under specified conditions. Weber's law approximates a constant proportional difference threshold within a sensory range. Signal detection separates sensitivity from the decision criterion; expectations and the costs of errors can shift that criterion.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Sensation & Perception. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.video2Note: Crash Course Psychology #5 — sensation, perception, and perceptual interpretation.
modules.practiceNote: Worked models: identical dots grouped as three close pairs with large gaps between pairs illustrate proximity; a broken outline perceived as a whole illustrates closure. A faint-tone observer who says yes more readily may have shifted criterion, not improved hearing. Practice: distinguish a hit, miss, false alarm, and correct rejection using signal-present and signal-absent trials; change one spacing or decision-cost condition and predict the result. Then complete the supplied fictional assignment; no login, paid service, or personal health disclosure is required.
modules.assignment: Analyze these four supplied perception cases: (A) an incomplete circle is still seen as whole; (B) two equal lines appear different beside converging rails; (C) a detector must decide whether a faint tone occurred amid noise; (D) a person notices the difference between 100 g and 120 g but not between 100 g and 105 g. Submit: a four-row analysis table plus a 250–350-word synthesis. Include: the best-matching concept for each case (closure, depth cue/size constancy, signal detection, or difference threshold/Weber's law), the stimulus information, the interpretation or decision, and one prediction if a key condition changes. Evaluation: The teacher checks concept-case accuracy, clear separation of sensation from perception, testable predictions, and correct use of threshold language.

modules.title: States of Consciousness
modules.objectives: Define consciousness, describe the stages of sleep and their functions, and explain the effects of psychoactive drugs on brain and behavior.
modules.readingNote: Read §4.2 for sleep functions, plus §4.1 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/4-1-what-is-consciousness for circadian rhythms, §4.3 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/4-3-stages-of-sleep for stages, §4.4 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/4-4-sleep-problems-and-disorders for sleep difficulties, and §4.5 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/4-5-substance-use-and-abuse for psychoactive drug effects. NREM N1 is light sleep, N2 includes spindles and K-complexes, and N3 has prominent slow delta activity. REM includes rapid eye movements, vivid dreaming, and reduced skeletal-muscle tone; both REM and NREM contribute to memory. Information-processing accounts emphasize memory organization; restoration accounts emphasize repair. Stimulants generally increase arousal, depressants reduce central nervous system activity, and hallucinogens alter perception. Agonists enhance or mimic transmitter effects; antagonists block receptor effects. These are descriptions, not instructions to use substances.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — States of Consciousness. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Worked distinction: memory consolidation is support for an information-processing account, whereas tissue restoration is a different proposed function. For narcolepsy, read the public MedlinePlus overview https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000802.htm : excessive daytime sleepiness and uncontrollable sleep episodes are central; REM regulation can be disrupted. Type 1 involves cataplexy and/or documented orexin deficiency; type 2 lacks cataplexy. REM intrusion alone is not a definition, and a brief diary cannot diagnose it. Practice: compute (6.0+7.5+5.5+8.0+6.5)/5, then explain why an alertness association does not prove sleep duration caused the difference. Then complete the supplied fictional assignment; no login, paid service, or personal health disclosure is required.
modules.assignment: Use this fictional five-night sleep record: 6.0, 7.5, 5.5, 8.0, and 6.5 hours; reported alertness scores are 4, 7, 3, 8, and 5 out of 10. Submit: a one-page data brief. Include: mean sleep duration, a correctly labeled line or bar graph, the observed association between sleep and alertness, two possible confounding variables, and a 250–350-word explanation connecting the pattern to sleep debt, circadian rhythm, and memory consolidation. State why this five-night record cannot diagnose a sleep disorder or prove causation. Evaluation: The teacher checks calculations, graph accuracy, correct concepts, evidence limits, and non-diagnostic wording. No personal sleep or health disclosure is required.

modules.title: Learning Theories
modules.objectives: Explain classical and operant conditioning with real-life examples, compare reinforcement schedules and their effects, and describe observational learning.
modules.readingNote: Read §6.2 for classical conditioning, extinction, generalization, and spontaneous recovery; §6.3 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning for the law of effect, reinforcement, punishment, and schedules; and §6.4 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-4-observational-learning for attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation. Classical conditioning associates stimuli; operant conditioning links behavior with consequences. Positive means adding a stimulus and negative means removing one; reinforcement increases behavior, punishment decreases it. Ratio schedules depend on response counts, interval schedules on elapsed time; fixed is predictable, variable changes.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Learning Theories. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.video2Note: YouTube — B. F. Skinner demonstrates teaching machines and programmed learning; use as historical context, not as a complete survey of reinforcement schedules.
modules.practiceNote: Worked schedule models: a reward after each five completed practice sets is fixed ratio; after an unpredictable number is variable ratio; the first response after each fixed week is fixed interval; the first response after varying delays is variable interval. Praising completed practice can reinforce it; removing an annoying reminder when practice begins can also reinforce it. Practice: classify each model and explain why an agreed reward contingent on completed practice differs from an improvised inducement to stop disruption. Model a missed day with supportive problem-solving rather than a penalty. Then complete the supplied fictional assignment; no login, paid service, or personal health disclosure is required.
modules.assignment: Design an ethical learning plan for this fictional case: Casey wants to complete twenty minutes of vocabulary practice on four school days each week but currently averages one day. Submit: a two-week behavior plan and a 350–450-word rationale. Include: a clearly defined target behavior, baseline, immediate positive reinforcer that does not involve money, an initial reinforcement schedule, criteria for moving to a thinner schedule, a simple tracking table, and a response to one missed day that is not punishment. Explain why each step is operant conditioning and distinguish reinforcement from bribery and punishment. Evaluation: The teacher checks operational definitions, schedule accuracy, ethical safeguards, measurable data, and correct application of conditioning principles.

modules.title: Memory Systems
modules.objectives: Describe the three-stage model of memory, explain encoding, storage, and retrieval processes, and identify common reasons for forgetting.
modules.readingNote: Read §8.1 for sensory, short-term/working, and long-term memory, encoding, storage, retrieval, chunking, and rehearsal; §8.3 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/8-3-problems-with-memory for encoding failure, retrieval problems, and interference; and §8.4 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/8-4-ways-to-enhance-memory for elaboration and retrieval practice. Working memory actively manipulates temporarily held information. Miller's historical 7 ± 2 estimate concerns span/chunking under particular tasks, not a universal working-memory limit. Primacy and recency describe better recall for early and late list items. Encoding specificity predicts better retrieval when useful encoding cues are reinstated.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Memory Systems. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.video2Note: Crash Course Psychology #13 — encoding, storage, retrieval, and memory errors.
modules.practiceNote: Worked model: repeating a definition is maintenance rehearsal; explaining it through a familiar example is elaboration. Recalling without looking is retrieval practice. An old password interfering with a new one is proactive interference; a new password interfering with an old one is retroactive interference. Practice: count recalled items/20 × 100 for each supplied condition, distinguish cue benefit from proof of permanent storage, and design a brief spaced self-test. Then complete the supplied fictional assignment; no login, paid service, or personal health disclosure is required.
modules.assignment: Use this supplied recall record for a 20-word list: immediate recall items 1,2,3,4,5,9,14,18,19,20; delayed recall without cues items 1,2,4,18,20; delayed recall after category cues items 1,2,4,5,9,14,18,19,20. Submit: a table, one graph, and a 350–450-word analysis. Include: recall percentages for each condition, evidence for primacy and recency, the effect of retrieval cues, one alternative explanation, and a study plan using elaborative encoding and retrieval practice. Evaluation: The teacher checks arithmetic, graph labels, accurate memory concepts, distinction between description and explanation, and a plan tied to the evidence.

modules.title: Thinking & Language
modules.objectives: Describe cognitive processes involved in problem-solving and decision-making, explain common cognitive biases and heuristics, and describe the relationship between language and thought.
modules.readingNote: Read §7.3 for algorithms, heuristics, functional fixedness, confirmation, availability, representativeness, and anchoring; §7.1 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/7-1-what-is-cognition for concepts; and §7.2 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/7-2-language for language and thought. Supplement: confirmation favors belief-consistent evidence; availability uses ease of recall; representativeness uses similarity to a prototype, sometimes ignoring base rates; anchoring gives undue weight to an initial value; framing changes judgments through different descriptions of equivalent outcomes. Algorithms specify a systematic solution procedure; heuristics are quicker shortcuts that can fail. Semantics concerns meaning; syntax concerns arrangement. Language can shape attention and categorization without determining every thought.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Thinking & Language. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Worked model: describing the same club result as 90% success or 10% failure changes framing, not the underlying rate. Judging event risk from one vivid failure is availability; searching only cancellation-friendly posts is confirmation; comparing costs to the first $4,000 proposal is anchoring. Practice: use comparable-event data to test the anchor, actively seek disconfirming evidence, and distinguish resemblance from actual frequency when estimating probabilities. Then complete the supplied fictional assignment; no login, paid service, or personal health disclosure is required.
modules.assignment: Use this fictional decision: A school club sees one dramatic news story about a failed outdoor event, ignores three years of local weather data, and keeps searching until it finds posts supporting cancellation. The first suggested budget was $4,000, so later members call $3,000 “cheap” even though comparable events cost $1,800. Submit: a 450–550-word decision memo. Include: identification and explanation of availability, confirmation, and anchoring effects; the exact case detail supporting each label; a debiasing step for each; and a revised evidence checklist the club should use. Evaluation: The teacher checks correct bias identification, evidence-to-claim links, feasible debiasing steps, and a decision process that does not assume the final choice in advance.

modules.title: Intelligence
modules.objectives: Define intelligence, compare major theories including Spearman's g, Gardner's multiple intelligences, and Sternberg's triarchic theory, and evaluate the role of heredity and environment in intelligence.
modules.readingNote: Read §7.4 for general intelligence, fluid/crystallized abilities, Gardner, and Sternberg; §7.5 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/7-5-measures-of-intelligence for reliability, validity, standardization, and the Flynn effect; and only the genetics/environment discussion in §7.6 https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/7-6-the-source-of-intelligence (the introductory life history is not assigned). Spearman's g summarizes shared variation across cognitive tasks; Sternberg distinguishes analytical, creative, and practical abilities; Gardner proposes multiple domains such as linguistic, musical, spatial, and bodily-kinesthetic abilities. Gardner's independent-domain proposal has less psychometric support than g and is not evidence for matching teaching to fixed learning styles. Fluid reasoning often declines across later adulthood while accumulated crystallized knowledge can remain stable or grow; these are group trends with individual variation. Heritability describes variation within a studied population/environment, not immutability or a percentage of one person's intelligence.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Intelligence. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Worked comparison: Avery's novel reasoning fits fluid/analytical ability but says little about practical application; Blake's original adaptation fits creative/practical proposals; Chen's correlated test strengths are consistent with g. A musical skill could fit Gardner's musical domain without proving all domains independent. Repeated stable scores indicate reliability; measuring the intended construct supports validity. The Flynn effect describes historical cohort score gains, not inevitable gains everywhere. Practice: apply all three theories to each profile, name what evidence is missing, and explain how schooling and opportunity can affect measured performance without assigning a fixed label. Then complete the supplied fictional assignment; no login, paid service, or personal health disclosure is required.
modules.assignment: Use these fictional profiles: Avery solves unfamiliar logic problems quickly but needs practice applying them in daily tasks; Blake designs original projects and adapts well to new settings but has average standardized scores; Chen performs strongly across vocabulary, spatial, and quantitative tests. Submit: a 500–650-word comparative brief applying Spearman's g, Sternberg's triarchic theory, and Gardner's multiple-intelligences proposal. Include: what each theory explains in each profile, one measurement or evidence limitation for each theory, the difference between reliability and validity, and a cautious recommendation for how a school should use multiple indicators. Evaluation: The teacher checks theory accuracy, use of all three profiles, measurement literacy, and avoidance of fixed or deterministic labels.

quizQuestions.question: Which perspective focuses on unconscious drives and early childhood experiences as determinants of behavior?
quizQuestions.explanation: The psychodynamic perspective, rooted in Freud's work, emphasizes unconscious processes and early life experiences.

quizQuestions.question: Wilhelm Wundt is best known for establishing the first scientific:
quizQuestions.explanation: Wundt opened the first experimental psychology laboratory in Leipzig, Germany in 1879.

quizQuestions.question: A researcher assigns students at random to study with music or silence and then compares recall scores. What is the manipulated independent variable?
quizQuestions.explanation: The researcher deliberately changes the study condition. Recall score is the dependent variable measured after that manipulation.

quizQuestions.question: Which part of the neuron receives incoming signals from other neurons?
quizQuestions.explanation: Dendrites are branch-like structures that receive incoming signals from other neurons.

quizQuestions.question: The process by which a neuron fires an electrical signal is called:
quizQuestions.explanation: An action potential is the electrical impulse that travels down the axon when a neuron fires.

quizQuestions.question: Which brain structure is primarily responsible for processing fear and emotional memories?
quizQuestions.explanation: The amygdala plays a central role in processing fear, threat detection, and emotional memories.

quizQuestions.question: A sudden alarm raises heart rate and breathing; after the alarm ends, the body gradually returns toward baseline. Which division chiefly supports that recovery?
quizQuestions.explanation: The parasympathetic division supports rest-and-digest functions that slow arousal and help the body return toward baseline after a threat passes.

quizQuestions.question: Weber's Law states that the just noticeable difference between two stimuli is:
options: A constant proportion of the original stimulus
quizQuestions.answer: A constant proportion of the original stimulus
quizQuestions.explanation: Weber's Law holds that the JND is a constant fraction of the stimulus intensity.

quizQuestions.question: The process by which sensory receptors convert physical energy into neural signals is called:
quizQuestions.explanation: Transduction is the conversion of physical stimuli (light, sound) into electrochemical neural signals.

quizQuestions.question: Identical dots have small gaps within pairs and much larger gaps between pairs. Which Gestalt principle best explains seeing separate pairs?
quizQuestions.explanation: Proximity groups elements that are near one another. All dots look alike, so relative spacing, rather than feature similarity or contour completion, distinguishes the pairs.

quizQuestions.question: REM sleep is primarily associated with:
options: Slow delta waves and deep rest
quizQuestions.explanation: REM (rapid eye movement) sleep is when vivid dreaming occurs and is linked to memory consolidation.

quizQuestions.question: Which account of sleep emphasizes consolidating and organizing daily experiences into memories?
quizQuestions.explanation: The information-processing theory of sleep suggests sleep helps consolidate and organize daily experiences into memory.

quizQuestions.question: A drug that mimics or increases the effect of a neurotransmitter is called an:
quizQuestions.explanation: Agonists bind to receptor sites and mimic or enhance the action of a neurotransmitter.

quizQuestions.question: Which stage of NREM sleep is characterized by slow delta waves and is hardest to wake from?
quizQuestions.explanation: Stage 3 NREM (slow-wave sleep) features delta waves and is the deepest, most restorative sleep stage.

quizQuestions.question: In classical conditioning, the neutral stimulus that comes to elicit a response after pairing is called the:
quizQuestions.explanation: After repeated pairings with the UCS, the neutral stimulus becomes the conditioned stimulus (CS).

quizQuestions.question: Thorndike's Law of Effect states that behaviors followed by satisfying consequences are:
quizQuestions.explanation: The Law of Effect is the foundation of operant conditioning: rewarded behaviors increase in frequency.

quizQuestions.question: A car stops beeping when the driver fastens the seat belt, making future fastening more likely. This is an example of:
quizQuestions.explanation: Fastening increases because it removes an unpleasant sound. Removing an aversive stimulus to strengthen behavior is negative reinforcement.

quizQuestions.question: A game rewards a player after an unpredictable number of completed challenges. Which reinforcement schedule is being used?
quizQuestions.explanation: The reward depends on a changing number of responses, so it is a variable-ratio schedule rather than a time-based schedule.

quizQuestions.question: In Atkinson-Shiffrin's model, information that is not attended to is lost from:
quizQuestions.explanation: Sensory memory holds information briefly; without attention it decays and is never transferred to short-term memory.

quizQuestions.question: Miller's Law states that short-term memory can hold approximately how many chunks of information?
quizQuestions.explanation: George Miller's famous paper proposed that STM capacity is 7 ± 2 chunks of information.

quizQuestions.question: The phenomenon where items at the beginning of a list are best recalled is called the:
quizQuestions.explanation: The primacy effect occurs because early list items have had more time for rehearsal and transfer to LTM.

quizQuestions.question: A student recalls more vocabulary in the same room where it was learned than in a different room. Which principle best explains the difference?
quizQuestions.explanation: Environmental context present during encoding can serve as a retrieval cue later, which is the core prediction of encoding specificity.

quizQuestions.question: The tendency to search for information that confirms our existing beliefs is called:
quizQuestions.explanation: Confirmation bias leads people to favor information that supports their existing views and ignore contradictory evidence.

quizQuestions.question: The availability heuristic leads people to judge likelihood based on:
options: How easily an example comes to mind
quizQuestions.answer: How easily an example comes to mind
quizQuestions.explanation: The availability heuristic is a mental shortcut where we assess probability by how quickly examples are recalled.

quizQuestions.question: A treatment is described as having a 90% survival rate to one group and a 10% mortality rate to another, even though the outcomes are identical. Different choices between the groups would best illustrate:
quizQuestions.explanation: Equivalent information can produce different judgments when it is framed in terms of gains versus losses.

quizQuestions.question: Spearman's 'g' factor refers to:
quizQuestions.explanation: Spearman's g is a general intelligence factor he believed underlies performance on all cognitive tasks.

quizQuestions.question: Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences includes which of the following types?
quizQuestions.explanation: Gardner proposed eight intelligences including linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, and bodily-kinesthetic among others.

quizQuestions.question: In Intelligence, The Flynn Effect refers to:
options: Rising average IQ scores across generations
quizQuestions.answer: Rising average IQ scores across generations
quizQuestions.explanation: The Flynn Effect is the documented rise in average IQ scores observed across many nations over the 20th century.

quizQuestions.question: An intelligence test gives nearly identical scores one week apart but does not predict performance in the tasks it claims to measure. The test is:
quizQuestions.explanation: Stable scores across time indicate reliability. Failure to predict the intended construct indicates weak validity despite that consistency.

questions.question: Which early school of psychology used introspection to study the basic elements of consciousness?
questions.explanation: Wundt and Titchener's structuralism used introspection to analyze the components of conscious experience.

questions.question: Which neurotransmitter is most associated with the reward pathway and motivation?
questions.explanation: Dopamine is central to the brain's reward system, regulating motivation, pleasure, and reinforcement learning.

questions.question: The absolute threshold is defined as the minimum stimulus intensity detected:
questions.explanation: The absolute threshold is the stimulus level detected 50% of the time under ideal conditions.

questions.question: Sleep deprivation is most likely to impair which type of memory
questions.explanation: Sleep is important for consolidating declarative memories such as facts and events.

questions.question: Extinction in classical conditioning occurs when:
options: The CS is repeatedly presented without the UCS
The UCS is presented without the CS
Reinforcement is removed from operant behavior
The organism generalizes the CS to other stimuli
questions.answer: The CS is repeatedly presented without the UCS
questions.explanation: Extinction weakens the conditioned response when the CS is presented repeatedly without the UCS.

questions.question: Elaborative rehearsal improves long-term memory retention compared to maintenance rehearsal because it:
questions.explanation: Elaborative rehearsal connects new information to existing knowledge, creating richer encoding and better retrieval cues.

questions.question: The framing effect demonstrates that decision-making is influenced by:
options: How information is presented rather than its content
questions.answer: How information is presented rather than its content
questions.explanation: Tversky and Kahneman showed that equivalent information framed as gains vs. losses leads to different decisions.

questions.question: Sternberg's triarchic theory divides intelligence into analytical, creative, and:
questions.explanation: Sternberg’s triarchic theory distinguishes analytical, creative, and practical intelligence; practical intelligence concerns adapting knowledge to everyday contexts.

questions.question: At a typical chemical synapse, what follows the arrival of an action potential at the presynaptic terminal?
options: The receiving neuron releases its myelin into the gap
Neurotransmitter is released and can bind receptors on the receiving cell
Dendrites carry the action potential backward along the sending axon
The synaptic gap closes to fuse the two neurons
questions.answer: Neurotransmitter is released and can bind receptors on the receiving cell
questions.explanation: M2 distinguishes electrical propagation along an axon from chemical signaling across a synapse; transmitter binding changes activity in the receiving cell.

questions.question: Before training, food elicits salivation and a tone does not. After tone–food pairings, the tone alone elicits salivation. Which labels are correct after training?
options: Tone: conditioned stimulus; salivation to tone: conditioned response
Tone: unconditioned stimulus; salivation to tone: unconditioned response
Food: conditioned stimulus; tone: conditioned response
Salivation to tone: conditioned stimulus; tone: unconditioned response
questions.answer: Tone: conditioned stimulus; salivation to tone: conditioned response
questions.explanation: M5: the initially neutral tone becomes a conditioned stimulus after association with food, and salivation to that tone is the conditioned response. Food remains an unconditioned stimulus; stimuli and responses are different parts of the sequence.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly distinguishes the central and peripheral nervous systems?
options: Central: brain and spinal cord; peripheral: nerves connecting them to the body
Central: all body nerves; peripheral: brain and spinal cord
Central: sympathetic nerves only; peripheral: parasympathetic nerves only
Central: voluntary motor nerves; peripheral: sensory cortex
questions.answer: Central: brain and spinal cord; peripheral: nerves connecting them to the body
questions.explanation: M2: the CNS contains the brain and spinal cord; the PNS connects it with sensory receptors, muscles, and organs. Sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions are parts of the autonomic PNS.

questions.question: Which explanation of studying most clearly uses the humanistic perspective introduced in M1?
options: Unconscious conflict determines the student’s choices
Neurotransmitter activity explains every study decision
Rewards alone maintain the study routine
The student chooses a meaningful goal and seeks personal growth
questions.answer: The student chooses a meaningful goal and seeks personal growth
questions.explanation: Humanistic approaches emphasize agency, meaning, and growth; the other accounts emphasize psychodynamic, biological, or behavioral mechanisms.

questions.question: A learner judges an event likely because one vivid example is easy to recall. Which shortcut is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: M7: availability uses ease of recall; representativeness uses resemblance to a typical case, anchoring uses an initial reference value, and functional fixedness limits imagined uses of objects.

questions.question: In M6, what is the term for interference when an old password makes it harder to remember a new password?
questions.explanation: Earlier learning interfering with newer learning is proactive interference; the reverse direction is retroactive interference.

questions.question: Which conclusion about heritability is justified by M8?
options: A high heritability estimate means education cannot affect scores
A heritability estimate states how much of one person’s score is genetic
Heritability concerns variation in a studied population under particular environments
Heritability proves that differences between any two groups are genetic
questions.answer: Heritability concerns variation in a studied population under particular environments
questions.explanation: Heritability is a population statistic conditioned on the range of genes and environments studied. It does not establish immutability or causes of between-group differences.

questions.question: Which research method allows researchers to establish cause-and-effect relationships?
questions.explanation: Experiments can support causal conclusions when variables are manipulated and confounds are controlled.

questions.question: The resting potential of a neuron is approximately:
questions.explanation: At rest, a neuron maintains a membrane potential of approximately -70 millivolts due to ion distribution.

questions.question: Signal detection theory accounts for the role of _______ in perception.
questions.explanation: Signal detection theory shows that perception involves both sensory sensitivity and decision criteria influenced by expectation and motivation.

questions.question: Which symptom pattern is central to the M4 account of narcolepsy?
options: Excessive daytime sleepiness with uncontrollable sleep episodes
Repeated pauses in breathing during sleep
Walking while partly asleep during NREM sleep
questions.answer: Excessive daytime sleepiness with uncontrollable sleep episodes
questions.explanation: M4: narcolepsy involves excessive daytime sleepiness and sleep episodes, often with REM dysregulation. Cataplexy is associated with type 1; type 2 lacks cataplexy. REM intrusion alone does not define every case, and symptoms require clinical evaluation.

questions.question: Spontaneous recovery in conditioning refers to:
options: Reappearance of an extinguished response after a rest period
The first pairing of a CS and UCS
Immediate loss of all learned behavior
questions.answer: Reappearance of an extinguished response after a rest period
questions.explanation: Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished response after time has passed.

questions.question: The testing effect refers to the finding that:
options: Tests increase anxiety and reduce learning
Repeatedly testing oneself improves long-term retention
Multiple choice tests are less effective than essays
Studying from notes is superior to flashcards
questions.answer: Repeatedly testing oneself improves long-term retention
questions.explanation: The testing (retrieval practice) effect shows that actively recalling information strengthens memory more than re-reading.

questions.question: The representativeness heuristic leads people to judge probability based on:
options: How closely something matches a typical example
questions.answer: How closely something matches a typical example
questions.explanation: The representativeness heuristic judges probability by similarity to a prototype, often ignoring base rate information.

questions.question: Across later adulthood, what broad pattern is often found for crystallized knowledge and fluid reasoning, with individual variation?
options: Both inevitably increase in every person
Crystallized knowledge may remain stable or grow while fluid reasoning often declines
Crystallized knowledge always disappears while fluid reasoning grows
Neither can be influenced by experience
questions.answer: Crystallized knowledge may remain stable or grow while fluid reasoning often declines
questions.explanation: M8 distinguishes accumulated knowledge from novel reasoning. These are population tendencies, not fixed predictions for an individual.

questions.question: In an experiment comparing recall after music versus silence, which variable is the measured outcome?
options: The rule used to assign participants
questions.explanation: M1: recall is the dependent variable; music versus silence is the manipulated independent variable. Assignment and predictions are design features, not measured recall outcomes.

questions.question: A reader uses sentence context to identify a smudged word. Which process best explains this?
questions.explanation: M3: expectations and context guide interpretation in top-down processing; bottom-up processing begins with stimulus features, and transduction converts physical energy into neural signals.

questions.question: A learner receives a reward after every five completed practice sets, regardless of time. Which schedule is this?
questions.explanation: M5: a fixed-ratio schedule requires a fixed number of responses. Interval schedules depend on time, and variable schedules change the requirement.

questions.question: A five-night record shows that longer sleep accompanies higher alertness. Which conclusion is supported?
options: Longer sleep was associated with higher alertness in this record
The record proves a sleep disorder caused low alertness
The record rules out stress and workload as confounds
Every student will show the same numerical relationship
questions.answer: Longer sleep was associated with higher alertness in this record
questions.explanation: M4 supports describing the observed association. With five observational records and no control of confounds, causation, diagnosis, and population-wide conclusions are not established.

questions.question: Which M6 memory process converts incoming information into a form that can be stored?
questions.explanation: Encoding prepares information for storage; storage maintains it and retrieval accesses it later.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly distinguishes two components of language taught in M7?
options: Semantics: meaning; syntax: rules for arranging words
questions.answer: Semantics: meaning; syntax: rules for arranging words
questions.explanation: Semantics concerns meaning, whereas syntax concerns the arrangement of words. Vocal properties and learning processes are different concepts.

questions.question: A test gives stable scores but fails to measure its claimed ability. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
options: It has strong validity because scores repeat
It is reliable but lacks evidence of validity
It must be valid because it has a numerical score
Its lack of validity proves scores cannot repeat
questions.answer: It is reliable but lacks evidence of validity
questions.explanation: M8: reliability is consistency and validity concerns the intended interpretation or construct. Consistency alone cannot establish that a test measures what it claims.

questions.question: Which memory system allows us to hold and mentally manipulate information for seconds to minutes?
questions.explanation: Working memory (Baddeley's model) is the active system for temporarily holding and manipulating information.

questions.question: Observational learning requires attention, retention, reproduction, and:
questions.explanation: Bandura's observational learning model includes attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation.

questions.question: Which shift best describes the cognitive revolution discussed in M1?
options: Eliminating all experiments in favor of introspection
Returning scientific attention to mental processes such as memory and thinking
Treating observable reinforcement as the only possible explanation
questions.answer: Returning scientific attention to mental processes such as memory and thinking
questions.explanation: The cognitive revolution made mental processes central to psychological research while retaining empirical methods, rather than limiting explanation to observable stimulus-response relations.

questions.question: Which event is reuptake, as taught in M2?
options: A transmitter binds a postsynaptic receptor
An axon fires an action potential
Released transmitter is taken back into the presynaptic cell
questions.answer: Released transmitter is taken back into the presynaptic cell
questions.explanation: Reuptake removes transmitter from the synaptic space by transporting it back into the releasing cell; it differs from receptor binding and electrical propagation.

questions.question: What M6 memory process accesses stored information when you recall a definition without looking?
questions.explanation: Retrieval accesses stored information. Recalling before checking notes is retrieval practice rather than mere rereading.
